summary: For ages 7–9, distinguish weather (what the atmosphere is doing now/today, changeable hour to hour) from climate (the typical long-run pattern of weather in a place, averaged over many years — roughly 30). The core idea is TIMESCALE and AGGREGATION: climate is the long-run average, weather is a single sample. Use the anchor phrase 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get', build climate from many days of real weather data settling into a stable average, and directly address the belief that one unusually cold (or hot) day changes or disproves the climate. Keep climate-change specifics light at this age, focusing on the weather/climate distinction itself.
misconceptions: 'A cold day (or snowstorm) means the climate isn't warming' — confusing one weather sample with the long-term trend
Weather and climate are synonyms / interchangeable words
Climate is just 'the weather somewhere far away or exotic' rather than the long-run average of any place's weather
Climate never changes / weather is totally random — both are patterns at different timescales

activities.title: Watch a climate form from many days of weather
steps: Step forward through a town's daily weather, one day at a time — a jittery mix of hot and cold days plotted as daily temperature points (rain can be tracked on a separate chart).
Watch a running-average line gradually settle into a steady band as more and more days accumulate.

Narrow a time window to just a few days and describe what you see (scattered, hard to predict = WEATHER); widen it to many years and describe how the long-run average and the usual seasonal pattern become steady and predictable (= CLIMATE).
Drop in one unusually freezing record-day and watch how much (or how little) the many-year average moves.
Switch to a second town and watch a different climate band form from its own weather, then compare the two towns' climates.
Say out loud, in your own words, why one cold day does not change the climate.
activities.insight: Climate is the long-run average of many days of weather; a single day is just one sample, so one cold or hot day barely shifts the multi-year average and cannot by itself tell you the climate.

activities.title: Today vs a typical year, side by side
steps: Look at a 'today' snapshot for a place (one day's weather) next to a 'typical year' summary for the same place.
Reveal labels and state which panel shows weather and which shows climate, and why.
Explain what you would need to collect — and over how long — to describe the climate of your own town.
activities.insight: Weather is a single-day snapshot of the atmosphere; climate is a summary of the typical pattern built from many years of such snapshots.

activities.title: Sort statements: weather or climate?
steps: Drag or write statements into two columns, WEATHER and CLIMATE (e.g. 'It is raining right now', 'Summers here are usually hot and dry', 'It snowed yesterday', 'This region is hot all year round').
Answer a trap item: a single record-hot (or record-cold) day — does that one day change the climate? Choose and justify.
Give your own example that shows one cold day doesn't change the overall climate.
activities.insight: Deciding whether each statement is about a single moment or a long-run average checks that the learner separates a single sample from the aggregated pattern, including rejecting the claim that one extreme day changes the climate.

activities.title: Question a climate expert about a cold snap
steps: Pose the question: 'Today there's a sudden cold snap — is that proof there's no warming?' and predict the answer before reading the reply.
Discuss follow-ups: 'Could two towns have the same weather today but different climates?' and 'A desert has a rainy day — has its climate stopped being a desert climate?'
Summarise, in your own words, what evidence would actually tell us about a place's climate.
activities.insight: Single weather events are weak evidence about climate; describing climate requires many years of averaged data and attention to trends, not individual days.

checkQuestion: One December morning it is unusually warm where you live. Your friend says, 'See — that proves the climate is changing.' Is one warm day good evidence about climate? Explain what would actually tell us about the climate.
checkAnswer: No — one warm day is weather, the day-to-day state of the atmosphere. Climate is the average pattern of weather over many years (about 30). To say anything about climate you need long-run averages and trends, not a single day.
